name: Maya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy frozen and chilled food for Fenwick Foodservice, which supplies cafes, canteens and care homes. I'm up at five to catch the market prices, then it's the phone and the spreadsheet all day. I came over from telesales six years ago and I still feel like the new girl on the desk. The worst part is a freezer failure at a supplier, because then I'm ringing round at night to replace forty pallets of chicken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. I'd tell the girls at work that every few years there's a new thing, and the phones still ring, and the lorries still need loading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not relaxed, hype or no hype. Fenwick lost a big care-home chain in the summer, and my mother's care home fees go up every January. Money's tight in ways AI has nothing to do with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, same as ever, and make sure I'm not the one who makes mistakes. I'd stay away from the new software my boss Dennis keeps mentioning, and I'd put 80 pounds a month aside for Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, in a steady sort of way. Like being a bit cold all the time, but not shivering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Fenwick lost a care-home contract. Does that touch your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It touches everyone a little, because when they lose volume they look at the overheads, and the buying desk is overheads. Dennis says we're safe, but he said that before they let two people go from the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How are you managing your mother's care fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We split it with my brother Hassan, about 600 pounds a month between us. Karim's wage from the garage covers the mortgage, and my pay covers the rest. If either one of us lost hours we'd have a problem.

say: I'd tell the girls the phones still **ring** and the lorries still need loading.
think: Money is tight for reasons that have nothing to do with AI, like my mother's **care fees**.
Fenwick lost a care-home chain, and the buying desk is **overhead**.
do: Carry on as ever and keep away from the **new software**.
Put aside **80 pounds** a month for my mother.
feel: **Tense** in a steady way, like being a bit cold all the time.
S0.quote: Money's tight in ways AI has nothing to do with.
fieldNote: Mood is driven by **existing** pressures: care fees and a lost contract.
Avoids the new software out of habit, not **argument**.
Her husband's garage wage covers the **mortgage**, her pay the rest.

steps.text: Keep buying the old way and double-check every order
Put 80 pounds a month aside for my mother's fees
Split the care home costs evenly with my brother Hassan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. I'd tell my friends I've seen a lot of clever ideas come and go, but I'd also keep quiet at work, because nobody likes the person who says it'll go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried. My junior status is the weak point, since I'm the one with six years and not twenty, and if they want to shrink the desk I'm the easy choice. I also don't use any of this stuff, and everybody can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dennis if the firm would teach me, slowly and in person, not just a video. I'd learn the minimum to keep up, and I'd keep my savings where they are. I would not go looking for another job at 58.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit ashamed. I don't like being the one who can't keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks would the software take, and which are you good at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The comparing of prices and the standing orders for the cafes, I'd think. What I'm good at is knowing which supplier's cod is really fresh and which cheats on the weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if Dennis told you to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, but I'd want it written that I won't be judged on speed while I learn. I'd also ask what happens to the people who can't pick it up, because that might be me.

say: I'd tell friends I've seen clever ideas come and go, but keep **quiet** at work.
think: My junior **status** is the weak point; with six years I'm the easy choice.
Everyone can see I don't use any of this **stuff**.
do: Ask Dennis for slow, **in-person** training, not just a video.
Learn the **minimum** to keep up and not look for another job.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit ashamed at being the one who can't keep up.
S1.quote: What I'm good at is knowing which supplier's cod is really fresh and which cheats on the weight.
fieldNote: Fear is of being **seen** as slow, not of the technology itself.
Sees her **supplier knowledge** as the thing worth protecting.
Wants it in writing that she won't be judged on **speed**.

steps.text: Ask Dennis for in-person training on the ordering software
Keep my savings where they are and watch the desk
Keep checking each supplier's fish by phone and weight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, not the companies, not the government. People in the middle like me will have to cope with whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm gone within the two years. I'm 58, I'm the junior, and I've never used AI. If the firm can buy a machine that does my work for the price of a subscription, I'd be out, and I'd be too old for anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd honestly probably freeze for a few weeks. After that I'd talk to Karim about me stopping at 60 and living off his wage and whatever I've saved. We have about three months saved, so that would mean selling the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky in the night, and flat in the day. I just don't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you think you'd be a year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be home, I think, with Mum's care home visits, and Karim carrying the money. Hassan would have to pay more. We'd be getting by, but only just, with no holidays and no new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should have seen it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone, and nobody. The government should have, the firms should have, but I wouldn't have seen it either. I'm cross, but I couldn't tell you who with.

say: I'd say nobody is **ready**, not companies or the government.
People in the middle like me will have to **cope**.
think: I think I'm gone within **two years**, with no AI experience and too old for anyone else.
A subscription costs less than my **wage**.
do: Freeze for a few weeks, then talk to Karim about **stopping** at 60.
Live on his wage and my savings, and sell the **car**.
feel: **Panicky** at night and flat in the day, with no idea where to start.
S2.quote: I'm 58, I'm the junior, and I've never used AI.
fieldNote: Describes a **freeze** reaction, not a plan.
Her husband's wage and her brother's **help** are the real safety net.

steps.text: Talk to Karim about me stopping work at 60
Sell our second car to cover three months
Ask Hassan to pay more of Mum's care fees
Wait to see whether Fenwick offers a redundancy deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people a fighting chance. I'd tell the younger girls to get their heads around it now, and not leave it to be like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be 63 by then, and I think I'd get to about 62 and be pushed out. It's the last few years that bother me, because that's when you can't recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the simplest tools, maybe on Saturdays at the library with a volunteer. I'd save as much as I could, probably 250 pounds a month, and I'd ask about an early pension at 62.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two year one. It's a slow dread, but I can breathe in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn the very basics. I got through a new till system in telesales and I swore I wouldn't. But I wouldn't be quick, and I'd need someone patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd really be able to learn it, or is that just a thing people say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. At 58 you've decided how you do things, and I'm no different. But a few lessons wouldn't kill me, and I'd rather try than sit there.

say: I'd say five years gives people a **fighting chance** if they use it well.
I'd tell the younger girls on the desk to learn it **now**.
think: I'd be **63**, and I think I'd be pushed out at about 62.
The last few years bother me because you can't **recover** then.
do: Learn the **simplest tools** on Saturdays at the library with a volunteer.
Save **250 pounds** a month and ask about an early pension at 62.
feel: Better than two years, a **slow dread** with room to breathe.
S3.quote: At 58 you've decided how you do things, and I'm no different.
fieldNote: Willing to try once there is **time** and a patient teacher.
Her admission of past **resistance** is honest and humble.

steps.text: Go to Saturday computer lessons at the library
Save 250 pounds a month from now
Ask the pension office about drawing early at 62

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long time, and the world will have worked something out. I'd say it's for the young people to worry about, and for the government to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a non-event. I'd be 68, retired, and probably babysitting. My worry would be my mother, who may not be here, and my kids and their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 65, stash away enough for six months, and then stop. I'd help my daughter Samira with her little ones and enjoy the garden. That's my plan, boring as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, actually, like watching rain from inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is past your retirement age. Would you still be anxious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still some anxiety, but about the pension, not the job. If the pension gets cut, then it matters a lot, because Karim and I have nothing else besides the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Fenwick to do for people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be honest early, and give older staff a decent send-off with some money. I don't need a medal, just fair notice and a fair package so I can step out gracefully.

say: I'd say ten years is long and the world will have worked something **out**.
I'd say it's for the **young** to worry about.
think: For me it's a **non-event**: I'd be 68 and retired.
My worry is my kids and their **jobs**.
do: Work to **65**, save about six months of expenses, then stop for good.
Help my daughter Samira with her **little ones** and enjoy the garden.
feel: Pretty **calm**, like watching rain from inside.
S4.quote: I don't need a medal, just fair notice and a fair package so I can step out gracefully.
fieldNote: Calm because her **age** puts her past the change.
Wants plain **fairness** from the employer, in notice and in the size of any package.

steps.text: Keep working at Fenwick until I turn 65
Build savings to six months before stopping
Help my daughter Samira with childcare in retirement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one, because I'd be too old to change and too young for my pension. What would help is fair notice, a proper package, and somebody patient to teach me, in person, with no one watching how slow I am.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that the people at my level aren't asked about any of this. We buy the food that feeds the care homes, and we get told about changes in a corridor.

headlineQuote: We buy the food that feeds the care homes, and we get told about changes in a corridor.
portrait: Maya is a **58-year-old** junior buyer of frozen and chilled food, up from telesales six years ago.
She has about **three months** saved, a husband Karim at a garage, and a mother whose care fees she helps pay.
Centre in outlook and **resistant** to technology, she has never used AI and fears looking slow.
Her mood is driven as much by **money pressures** as by AI, so even the mild case makes her uneasy.
She freezes in the worst case, then plans to **stop at 60** and lean on her husband and brother.
biggestWorry: The **two year** case, when she'd be too old to change and too young for her pension.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair notice**, a proper package and patient in-person teaching.
